Field surveys of Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) in the Luebecker Bucht population provide detailed morphometric data on the species. Newly emerged fry, which hatch after an incubation period of 8 days [ab = 8 days] at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], measure approximately 0.70 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.70 centimeters] in total length. This initial size is remarkably small, reflecting the reduced yolk reserves typical of teleost larvae that must rapidly transition to exogenous feeding. The calculated wet weight at this early stage is derived from a length-weight relationship, yielding a neonatal mass of roughly 0.003417 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.003417 grams], a value that underscores the vulnerability of the newly hatched alevin to predation and starvation. The brief embryonic development observed at this thermal regime is consistent with the rapid life-history pace of this species in northern European brackish habitats.

As the fish progress through the juvenile phase, considerable somatic growth occurs before the onset of sexual maturation. In the Luebecker Bucht population, individuals attain a standard length of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters] at puberty, a threshold that typically coincides with the completion of fin ray ossification and the acquisition of adult coloration. At this point, the wet weight at puberty averages 0.831 grams [Wwp = 0.831 grams], a mass that reflects substantial investment in axial musculature and visceral organs. The ultimate standard length recorded for this population is 8.0 centimeters [Li = 8.0 centimeters], though when measured as total length, including the caudal fin, adults reach a slightly larger value of 8.98 centimeters [Li = 8.98 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 7.213 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.213 grams]. These asymptotic dimensions suggest that indeterminate growth continues at a diminished rate after maturity, with most energy eventually directed toward reproduction rather than further elongation.

Reproductive output in Gasterosteus aculeatus has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions, revealing a notably high capacity for iteroparous spawning. Females maintain a maximum clutch frequency of approximately 160 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 160 clutches per year] when held at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Each spawning event typically produces around one egg per clutch [N_R_i = around one egg per clutch], though clutch size can vary with female body condition and age. These parameters indicate that an individual female is capable of generating roughly 160 offspring per year, a figure that underscores the species' r-selected reproductive strategy. The high thermal dependence of this reproductive rate is evident when comparing populations from different latitudinal zones, with cooler temperatures substantially reducing the frequency of consecutive spawning events.

The lifespan of the Three-spined stickleback is constrained by both thermal regime and ecological pressures. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded longevity is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], though wild populations seldom achieve this age due to predation and seasonal resource limitation. The first successful reproduction event occurs at 122 days after hatching [tR = 122 days after hatching] when fish are reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a remarkably early maturation that allows multiple cohorts to contribute to the breeding population within a single growing season. This abbreviated generation time, combined with sustained reproductive output, facilitates rapid population recovery after environmental perturbations, a trait that may explain the species' broad ecological success across diverse freshwater and brackish habitats throughout the Holarctic.

Predation risk and habitat complexity impose strong selective pressures on the antipredator morphology of Gasterosteus aculeatus. The development of lateral bony plates and dorsal spines is energetically costly, and trade-offs between somatic growth and armor production are well documented. In populations with high piscivore density, juveniles delay the onset of reproductive activity to allocate more resources toward structural defenses, often resulting in a larger size at first reproduction than observed in low-predation environments. Individual variation in plate morph frequency across populations correlates with salinity gradients, with fully plated morphs dominating in marine habitats while low-plated forms prevail in isolated freshwater streams. These morphological responses to local ecological conditions highlight the remarkable phenotypic plasticity of this species, which has made it a model organism for studies of parallel evolution and contemporary adaptation in post-glacial environments.
